newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's DAX streak seeks to regain momentum.
newsitem.headline: Germany's DAX streak seeks to regain momentum.

text.p: Germany's DAX index took a real beating at the start of trade on Monday, falling as much as four percent at one stage, but managed to halve its losses by the close amid hopes that the market's uptrend would remain intact, dealers and analysts said.

The blue-chip DAX index, catching up to Friday's Wall Street slump, finished 74.26 points or 1.79 percent lower to 4,078.60 after sliding by as much as 176 points or 4.2 percent earlier in the volatile session.

The DAX, which hit a lifetime intra-day high of 4,459.89 less than three weeks ago, has lost 381.29 points since touching that peak on July 31 as investors worried about higher interest rates, a weakening dollar and volatile U.S. shares.

But many believe German bourse will soon resume its upward trend and keep outperforming the U.S. market, where the Dow index has risen less than 30 percent so far this year. From the beginning of 1997 to the close on Monday, the DAX has risen by 41 percent.
"We assume that we will see the DAX index rising to about 4,700 points within nine to 12 months," said Christoph Benner at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Frankfurt.
The mark is a major factor supporting German shares as a the weak German currency makes exports more competitive, helping the country's fledgling recovery to take hold.
Expectations that both the German and U.S. central banks will not raise interest rates following their respective policy meetings this week, should also help market sentiment.
Still, some dealers said the German share market may not yet have found a solid foundation at the moment and could remain vulnerable to adverse movements on Wall Street.
"The DAX should spend the week bouncing around 4,000 points," said Ingo Mainert at Commerzbank in Frankfurt.
Mainert said, however, there was no parallel between the DAX's rocky condition and the 1987 market crash.
"We are merely seeing a correction after the historically high levels we have reached, just as occurred in 1986 and 1994," he said, noting other market corrections that occurred before fresh gains.
"The fundamentals are intact. This is a healthy correction, which may last several weeks. It would be normal for the market to fall 10 to 15 percent from its peak," he said.
But some market observers believe the DAX has seen its peak for now and do not look for an assault on record levels anytime soon.
"We see the market trading between 4,000 and 4,500 points in the coming months. So we see no chance for new record highs in the next few months," he said.
Others disputed that view, saying there was been no fundamental change in the market's condition to warrant further losses beyond the current consolidation phase.
"We do not think that this is a fundamental change in the market but instead a consolidation period that was necessary.
"There's no threat of a recession and corporate profits are growing moderately," said Christian Heger at Trinkaus Capital Management in Duesseldorf.
Heger said the market has "ideal conditions" and predicts the DAX will find support at the 3,950 level before ending the year at around 4,100.
Juergen Callies at Vereinsbank in Munich believes the DAX will end the week above Monday's closing level. "The bull market factors remain. Our six-month outlook remains intact at 4,600 points."
--Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525
